content: The mention of any company or product name does not imply endorsement by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). The exchange rate refers to the increment or decrement in decibels that necessitates halving or doubling the exposure time, respectively. For instance, a 3-dB exchange rate requires halving the noise exposure time for every 3-dB increase in noise level, while a 5-dB exchange rate requires halving the exposure time for every 5-dB increase. The term fence is used to describe the hearing threshold level above which a material impairment of hearing is considered to have occurred. Frequency, in the context of a periodic function in time, is defined as the reciprocal of the period. The hearing threshold level (HTL) is the amount, measured in decibels, by which the hearing threshold for a listener exceeds a specified reference equivalent threshold level for a given signal. Impulse is defined as the product of a force and the time during which the force is applied. Specifically, it is the time integral of force from an initial time to a final time. Impulsive noise is characterized by a sharp rise and rapid decay in sound levels, typically lasting less than one second. For the purposes of this document, it refers to impact or impulse noise. Intermittent noise refers to noise levels that are interrupted by intervals of relatively low sound levels. Noise is defined as (1) undesired sound or (2) any unwarranted disturbance within a useful frequency band, such as undesired electric waves in a transmission channel or device. It can also refer to erratic, intermittent, or statistically random oscillations. The noise reduction rating (NRR) is a single-number rating that indicates the noise reduction capabilities of a hearing protector. It is legally required to be displayed on the label of each hearing protector sold in the United States. The unit of measurement is decibels (dB). Permanent threshold shift (PTS) refers to a permanent increase in the threshold of audibility for an ear, resulting in irreversible hearing loss. Pulse range is the difference in decibels between the peak level of an impulsive signal and the root-mean-square level of continuous noise. A significant threshold shift is defined as a change in hearing threshold outside the range of audiometric testing variability (±5 dB) that necessitates follow-up action to prevent further hearing loss. NIOSH defines a significant threshold shift as an increase in the HTL of 15 dB or more at any frequency (500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, or 6000 Hz) in either ear, confirmed by a second test within 30 days. Sound is defined as (1) oscillation in pressure, stress, particle displacement, particle velocity, etc., in a medium with internal forces (e.g., elastic or viscous), or the superposition of such propagated oscillations, and (2) the auditory sensation evoked by the described oscillation. Sound intensity is the average rate of sound energy transmitted in a specified direction at a point through a unit area normal to this direction. The unit is watts per square meter (W/m²), and the symbol is I. Sound intensity level is ten times the logarithm to the base ten of the ratio of the intensity of a given sound in a stated direction to the reference sound intensity of 1 picowatt per square meter (pW/m²). The unit is decibels (dB), and the symbol is L. Sound pressure is the root-mean-square instantaneous sound pressure at a point during a given time interval. The unit is Pascal (Pa). Sound pressure level is defined as (1) ten times the logarithm to the base ten of the ratio of the time-mean-square pressure of a sound, in a stated frequency band, to the square of the reference sound pressure in gases of 20 micropascals (µPa). The unit is decibels (dB), and the symbol is Lp. For sound in media other than gases, unless otherwise specified, the reference sound pressure is 1 µPa. Temporary threshold shift (TTS) refers to a temporary increase in the threshold of audibility for an ear caused by exposure to high-intensity acoustic stimuli. This shift may also be caused by other factors, such as the use of aspirin or other drugs. The unit is decibels (dB). Time-weighted average (TWA) is the averaging of different exposure levels during an exposure period. For example, the formula 0 x Log (D/100) + 85, where D = dose, is used to calculate TWA. For an 8-hour work shift, the recommended exposure limit (REL) is a TWA of 85 dBA using a 3-dB exchange rate. Daily noise dose is calculated when daily noise exposure consists of periods of different noise levels. The daily dose (D) should not equal or exceed 100%, as calculated using the formula D = [C1/T1 + C2/T2 + ... + Cn/Tn] x 100, where C = total time of exposure at a specified noise level, and T = exposure duration for which noise at this level becomes hazardous. Noise exposure assessment must be conducted when any worker's 8-hour TWA exposure equals or exceeds 85 dBA. Measurements should conform to the American National Standard Measurement of Occupational Noise Exposure (ANSI S12.19-1996). Noise exposure is measured without regard to the use of hearing protectors. Initial monitoring is required when a new Hearing Loss Prevention Program (HLPP) is initiated. This involves assessing noise exposure levels representative of all workers whose 8-hour TWA noise exposures may equal or exceed 85 dBA. For stationary, continuous noise levels, a sound level meter or dosimeter may be used. For workers with intermittent or varying noise levels, a task-based exposure monitoring strategy may provide a more accurate assessment. Periodic monitoring must be repeated at least every two years if any worker's 8-hour TWA exposure equals or exceeds 85 dBA. Monitoring must also be repeated within three months of changes in equipment, production processes, or maintenance routines. Instrumentation used to measure workers' noise exposures must be calibrated to ensure accuracy and conform to ANSI standards. All continuous, varying, intermittent, and impulsive sound levels from 80 to 140 dBA must be integrated into noise measurements. Engineering controls, administrative controls, and work practices should be implemented to ensure workers are not exposed to noise at or above 85 dBA as an 8-hour TWA. Hearing protectors must be provided at no cost to workers when these controls cannot reduce exposure below 85 dBA. For TWA exposures exceeding 105 dBA, hearing protectors are necessary to supplement other controls. Audiometric testing must be performed by qualified professionals and include air-conduction, pure-tone hearing threshold measurements at specified frequencies. Baseline audiograms must be obtained before employment or within 30 days of employment for workers enrolled in the HLPP. Workers must not be exposed to noise levels at or above 85 dBA for at least 12 hours before baseline testing. Annual audiometric testing is required for all workers enrolled in the HLPP. Monitoring audiograms must be examined immediately to detect any significant threshold shifts. If a persistent threshold shift is confirmed, the worker must be informed, and follow-up actions must be taken to prevent further hearing loss. Exit audiograms should be obtained for workers leaving employment or no longer exposed to hazardous noise. These should be conducted under the same conditions as baseline audiometry. Warning signs must be clearly visible in areas where noise exposures routinely equal or exceed 85 dBA as an 8-hour TWA. Workers must be informed about the potential consequences of noise exposure and methods to prevent noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL). Employers must implement a training program in occupational hearing loss prevention for all workers exposed to noise at or above 85 dBA as an 8-hour TWA. Training must be repeated annually and updated to reflect changes in protective equipment and work processes. The effectiveness of the HLPP must be evaluated annually at both the individual worker and programmatic levels. Significant threshold shifts presumed to be occupationally related must be addressed to prevent additional hearing loss.
